Estimate grid-resolution data from grouped observations

Source: R/harmonise-ungroup.R
mt_ungroup.Rd

Fills the modelling grid (single years of age by default) from deaths and exposures observed in coarser age groups. The default is the penalized composite link model (PCLM; Eilers 2007; Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015) as published: the estimates are the fitted values of the model, without rescaling.

Usage

mt_ungroup(
  data,
  age = NULL,
  dims = 1,
  method = c("pclm", "monotone", "hyman_kannisto", "natural_gompertz", "gam"),
  exposure_method = c("pclm", "monotone"),
  lambda = NULL,
  criterion = c("bic", "aic"),
  kr = 2,
  deg = 3,
  pord = 2,
  lambda_range = c(0.01, 1e+08),
  preserve_totals = FALSE,
  open_split = c("pclm", "stationary"),
  tail = c("kannisto", "gompertz"),
  tail_width = 2
)

Arguments

data

An mt_data object.

age

Target age axis (mt_axis). By default the grid when it was set (with mt_set_grid() or step_grid()) and is finer than the data, otherwise single years of age from the lowest age to the start of the open interval.

dims

1 or 2 (for method = "pclm"; "gam" is always 2D, the other methods 1D).

method

Method for deaths: "pclm" (default), or "monotone", the monotone cubic interpolation of Hyman (1983) of the cumulative deaths (counts only, 1D, ignores exposures; group totals reproduced exactly). Deprecated, without a published source: "hyman_kannisto" (monotone spline of log group rates with a Kannisto tail), "natural_gompertz" (natural spline with a log-linear tail) and "gam" (2D tensor-product GAM of log group rates over age and year with a Kannisto tail, package mgcv); they need exposures on the grid and rescale to the exposure-weighted group rates. The vignette "Ungrouping age groups: methods and diagnostics" compares methods on data with known single years; mt_plot_ungroup() and mt_ungroup_check() check a result.

exposure_method

"pclm" or "monotone" (Hyman 1983).

lambda

Fixed smoothing parameter(s); NULL selects them by criterion.

criterion

"bic" or "aic".

kr

Knot spacing in years (age and period).

deg, pord

Degree of the B-splines and order of the difference penalty.

lambda_range

Search range for the smoothing parameters.

preserve_totals

Rescale the estimates to the observed group totals after the fit (default FALSE, the published PCLM); see Details.

open_split

Split of the exposure of an open interval of the grid when deaths are ungrouped as rates: "pclm" (default, the PCLM of the exposures, Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015) or "stationary" (package-specific stationary-population weights); see Details.

tail, tail_width

For the deprecated method = "gam": the parametric curve that takes over from the GAM above the start of the last age group ("kannisto", logistic, or "gompertz", log-linear), fitted to the GAM rates from age 70, and the width (years) of the logistic blend between the two.

Value

An mt_data object with deaths (and exposures) on the grid. Diagnostics per fit are attached as attribute "ungroup": smoothing parameters, effective dimension, the largest relative difference between fitted and observed group totals (before any rescaling), the number of iterations of the open-interval weights (open_iterations, NA without an expanded open interval), and a flag when a smoothing parameter is at the boundary of the search range.

Details

  • Exposures observed coarser than the grid are ungrouped first, as counts by the PCLM (exposure_method = "pclm") or by the monotone cubic interpolation of Hyman (1983) applied to the cumulative counts ("monotone"), which reproduces the group totals exactly.

  • Deaths are ungrouped as rates when exposures are available on the grid: the exposures enter the composite link as offset (Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015), so cohort-size waves stay in the exposures and the estimated rate schedule is smooth. Without exposures, deaths are ungrouped as counts per year of age (1D only; 2D smoothing of death counts cannot represent cohort waves and is refused).

  • dims = 1 fits each stratum and period separately; dims = 2 fits a smooth age-period surface of rates per stratum with two smoothing parameters, the PCLM of rates over age and period with exposures of Rizzi et al. (2019).

Group totals. The PCLM reproduces the total over all groups of a fit (the penalty leaves the level of the latent curve free), but not each group total: the gap is reported as max_rel_diff in the diagnostics. With preserve_totals = TRUE the estimates within each observed group are rescaled to the observed total after the fit, so that aggregation reproduces the data exactly. This rescaling is a post-hoc step of mortensor without a published source: it creates steps at the group boundaries, and with dims = 2 it puts the year-to-year noise of every group back onto the smooth surface. On England and Wales men (2000-2011, 5-year groups) the median absolute difference of the single-year log rates between the two settings is about 0.002 with dims = 1 and 0.008 with dims = 2.

Open age interval. For counts (exposures, or deaths without exposures), an open last group is expanded into single years up to the maximum age omega (see mt_data()) and the PCLM spreads its total over them, as with a last interval of width omega minus its lower bound in the ungroup package. For rates, an open interval of the grid (for example 100+) is expanded into single years up to omega as well, and its exposure is split over these years (open_split):

  • "pclm" (default): by the PCLM of the exposures of all grid cells, with a group of 0 counts of 15 years beyond omega, as Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers (2015) ungroup grouped exposures (their maximum age 115 and a group 115-130 with 0 counts); the estimates enter the composite link of the rates;

  • "stationary": with stationary-population weights l(x) = exp(-cumsum(m(x))) implied by the fitted rates; starting from rates that rise by 10% per year of age, the weights and the fit are iterated until no weight changes by more than 1e-6 (at most 50 iterations; the smoothing parameters are selected again once the weights have converged). This treatment is specific to mortensor (reference unknown); it was the default up to E3.

On French women and men (1997-2006, deaths in 5-year groups and 90+, grid open at 100+), the rate of 100+ was too high by 0.14 (women) and 0.15 (men) on the log scale with "stationary" and by 0.12 and 0.15 with "pclm"; the median absolute log error at 90-99 was 0.020 and 0.022 with "stationary", 0.019 and 0.022 with "pclm". On data simulated with the exposures of a stationary population above 100 (mt_example()), "stationary" was closer (median absolute log error at 90+ 0.006, against 0.009 with "pclm"), because that generator has the stationary exposures this option assumes.

Relation to Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers (2015). As in the paper, the observed counts are Poisson with means composed from a latent distribution exp(B beta) (times the exposures for rates), estimated by penalised likelihood with a second-order difference penalty on the coefficients weighted by lambda (their penalised log-likelihood with lambda / 2, by iteratively reweighted least squares), and the effective dimension is the trace of the hat matrix. The departures:

  • basis: the paper uses one coefficient per fine cell (B the identity) and allows a B-spline basis; here B is a cubic B-spline basis, as in Eilers (2007) and the ungroup package;

  • smoothing parameter: the paper minimises AIC over a grid of log10 lambda; the default here is BIC, the default of the ungroup package, minimised by golden-section search on log10 lambda within lambda_range. criterion = "aic" gives the paper's criterion;

  • open last interval of counts: the paper sets a maximum age (115) and adds a group with 0 counts beyond it (115-130); here the open group ends at omega without such a group. On French women in 2006 with exposures in 5-year groups and 90+, adding a group with 0 counts of 15 years beyond omega = 110 changed the median absolute log error of the rates at 90-109 from 0.19 (too low) to 0.66 (too high); with exposures in single years to 89 and 90+, from 0.57 to 0.14. The split of a wide open group from its total is weakly identified either way;

  • exposures: as in the paper, they enter the composite link, and grouped exposures are ungrouped by the PCLM first; the open interval of the grid as described above ("pclm" follows the paper);

  • iterations: the paper iterates until the coefficients change by less than 1e-6; here the iterations stop when the largest change is below 1e-6 relative to the coefficients or the penalised deviance changes by less than 1e-8 relative, with step halving when it rises;

  • in 2D (Rizzi et al. 2019) see Defaults below.

When the deaths are grouped more coarsely than the exposures at old ages (for example deaths 90+ and single-year exposures), the rates within the last group are extrapolated by the smooth latent curve from the lower groups, and the comparison with real data is poor at the highest ages. On French women in 2006 (Human Mortality Database data in the demography package), with deaths in 5-year groups and 90+ and exposures in single years to 110+, the median absolute log error of the ungrouped rates at ages 90-109 against the single-year rates was 0.09 with dims = 1 (0.02 at ages 30-89). The errors were within 0.1 on the log scale up to age 101, but the rates were too high by 0.3-0.4 at ages 104-109, because the latent curve continues the rise of the rates below 90 while the observed rates rise more slowly at the highest ages. With a grid open at 100+ (exposures 100+), the rate of 100+ was too high by 0.14 on the log scale (median over 1997-2006, see above). With the exposures also grouped in 5-year groups and 90+, the error at 90-109 was 0.19 (rates too low). With dims = 2 (1997-2006, ages 30 and over) and smoothing parameters chosen by BIC, the error at 90-109 was 1.4: BIC chose very small smoothing parameters (the large counts vary more than Poisson noise) and the rates inside the wide last group oscillated; with lambda = c(100, 10) fixed it was 0.05. Treat ungrouped rates inside a wide open group as extrapolations, prefer data with a higher open age, check the smoothing parameters (attribute "ungroup") and the result with mt_plot_ungroup().

Cells already observed at grid resolution are kept. When deaths are ungrouped as rates and the grid starts with age 0 as its own interval, an observed first year of life is kept and left out of the fit, as in mt_smooth(): infant mortality does not follow the age pattern of the following ages, and its peak would spill into ages 1-6.

Defaults. The basis and penalty follow the defaults of the ungroup package (version 1.6.3) for one dimension: cubic B-splines (deg = 3) with a knot every kr = 2 years, a second-order difference penalty (pord = 2) and the smoothing parameter chosen by BIC. The search range of the smoothing parameter is wider than ungroup's (0.1 to 1e5 in one dimension, 0.1 to 1000 in two): lambda_range = c(1e-2, 1e8). In two dimensions ungroup uses fixed smoothing parameters (1, 1) and a knot every 7 cells by default; here both parameters are chosen by BIC with a knot every kr years and periods.

The methods "hyman_kannisto", "natural_gompertz" and "gam" are deprecated: they are heuristics of this package without a published source. They still work, with a warning of class mt_warning_deprecated.

In backtests use step_ungroup() so that ungrouping, in particular in 2D, sees only the training window.

References

Eilers PHC (2007). Ill-posed problems with counts, the composite link model and penalized likelihood. Statistical Modelling 7(3): 239-254.

Hyman JM (1983). Accurate monotonicity preserving cubic interpolation. SIAM Journal on Scientific and Statistical Computing 4(4): 645-654.

Rizzi S, Gampe J, Eilers PHC (2015). Efficient estimation of smooth distributions from coarsely grouped data. American Journal of Epidemiology 182(2): 138-147. doi:10.1093/aje/kwv020

Rizzi S, Halekoh U, Thinggaard M, Engholm G, Christensen N, Johannesen TB, Lindahl-Jacobsen R (2019). How to estimate mortality trends from grouped vital statistics. International Journal of Epidemiology 48(2): 571-582. doi:10.1093/ije/dyy183

See also

mt_plot_ungroup() and mt_ungroup_check() for diagnostics.

Examples

x <- mt_example(years = 2010:2014)
u <- mt_ungroup(x)
u
#> <mt_data> 2 strata by sex, omega = 110
#>   deaths     single years 30-99, 100+; periods 2010-2014 (width 1); 710 cells
#>   exposure   single years 30-99, 100+; periods 2010-2014 (width 1); 710 cells
#>   grid       <mt_axis: age, 71 intervals> 30 31 32 33 ... 98 99 100+
#>              <mt_axis: period, 5 intervals> 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014
head(attr(u, "ungroup"))
#>    measure stratum period       method lambda_age lambda_period       ed
#>     <char>   <int> <char>       <char>      <num>         <num>    <num>
#> 1:  deaths       1   2010 pclm_rate_1d  18319.323            NA 6.511396
#> 2:  deaths       1   2011 pclm_rate_1d  27689.910            NA 6.082495
#> 3:  deaths       1   2012 pclm_rate_1d   7709.080            NA 7.443061
#> 4:  deaths       1   2013 pclm_rate_1d   2190.986            NA 8.906068
#> 5:  deaths       1   2014 pclm_rate_1d   1862.519            NA 9.109098
#> 6:  deaths       2   2010 pclm_rate_1d  18106.191            NA 6.839731
#>    max_rel_diff at_bound open_iterations open_converged
#>           <num>   <lgcl>           <int>         <lgcl>
#> 1:   0.05830036    FALSE              NA             NA
#> 2:   0.06314078    FALSE              NA             NA
#> 3:   0.04830307    FALSE              NA             NA
#> 4:   0.06514775    FALSE              NA             NA
#> 5:   0.02661996    FALSE              NA             NA
#> 6:   0.04527347    FALSE              NA             NA
# rescaled to the observed group totals (post-hoc step of the package)
ut <- mt_ungroup(x, preserve_totals = TRUE)
